row.basis: gain the world, forfeit the life
row.note: The commentary makes the trader's final capital his own self; Jesus asks what profit the whole world brings if a person forfeits his life, making the apparent gain a net personal loss.

row.basis: gain world, lose self
row.note: The commentary reads loss of one's self as the last entry in the account; this verse explicitly asks what benefit remains when a person gains the world but loses or forfeits himself.

row.basis: former gains counted loss
row.note: The commentary distinguishes apparent accumulation from the true balance; Paul says things once counted as gains became loss for Christ, reversing his own ledger.

row.basis: all things loss, Christ gain
row.note: The commentary's trade between perishing capital and lasting gain has a close counterpart in Paul's reckoning of everything as loss compared with gaining Christ.

row.basis: profit from toil under the sun
row.note: The commentary joins time, work and the merchant's question about real gain; Ecclesiastes asks what profit a human has from all the toil he toils under the sun.

row.basis: root table ع م ل / Hebrew עמל, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary puts a lifetime's work in the loss account; the speaker surveys works done by his hands and the עמל spent on them, finding no lasting profit under the sun.

row.basis: counting days for wisdom
row.note: The commentary treats passing time as spent capital; the psalm asks God to teach humans to number their days so that they gain a wise heart.

row.basis: brief years filled with toil
row.note: The commentary's late day and dwindling lifetime meet this psalm's seventy or eighty years, their toil and trouble, and their swift passing.

row.basis: riches fail on day of wrath
row.note: The commentary contrasts counted money with the final moral account; the proverb says riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death.

row.basis: ill-gotten treasure versus righteousness
row.note: The commentary's profitable trade through right action meets the proverb's claim that wicked treasure yields no profit but righteousness rescues from death.

row.basis: stored wealth, life required tonight
row.note: The commentary sets money counted as increase against the loss of the owner himself; God asks the rich fool whose stored goods will be his when his life is demanded that night.

row.basis: self-stored treasure versus true wealth
row.note: The commentary describes a hidden deficit while possessions grow; Jesus concludes that one who stores treasure for himself can fail to be rich toward God.

row.basis: imagined wealth, unrecognized poverty
row.note: The commentary stresses a loss one does not feel; Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing while failing to know its poverty and blindness.

row.basis: Moses notices fire in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary follows Moses noticing fire on a journey and seeking guidance; Exodus places the divine fire in a bush that burns without being consumed, specifying the sight he is drawn to investigate.

row.basis: Moses turns to inspect unconsumed bush
row.note: In the commentary's Qur'anic scene Moses hopes for an ember or guide for his family; in Exodus he turns aside to inspect why the burning bush is not consumed, a different immediate purpose for approaching the fire.

row.basis: unjust measures and weights prohibited
row.note: The commentary's seller secretly reduces the buyer's portion; Leviticus forbids injustice in measures of length, weight and quantity, grounding the market image in a concrete legal rule.

row.basis: two different weights in one bag
row.note: The commentary describes one trader using different scales depending on whether he takes or gives; Deuteronomy forbids keeping a large and a small weight together in one's bag.

row.basis: small measure, great price, false balances
row.note: The commentary's two-directional fraud matches merchants in Amos who shrink the ephah, enlarge the shekel and falsify balances while selling grain.

row.basis: false balance versus just weight
row.note: The commentary joins fair weighing to moral truth; the proverb calls a false balance abominable to the Lord and a just weight his delight.

row.basis: God weighs the person on a just balance
row.note: The commentary moves from market scales to the weighing of a person's own worth; Job asks that God weigh him in a just balance and know his integrity.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Aramaic חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary joins a deficient balance to personal loss; Daniel interprets TEKEL as the king weighed in the balances and found חַסִּיר, lacking.

row.basis: king weighed and found wanting
row.note: The commentary's final scale finds the person himself light rather than a short measure of goods; Daniel pronounces that the king has been weighed and found deficient.

row.basis: way seeming right ends in death
row.note: The commentary's gravest loser believes his work is good while straying; this proverb says a way can seem right to a person yet end in the ways of death.

row.basis: all people straying like sheep
row.note: The commentary says its judgment first includes the whole human kind and describes loss as going astray; Isaiah says all like sheep have strayed, each turning to his own way.

row.basis: all turned aside, none doing good
row.note: The commentary's generic human is under a negative verdict before an exception is named; the psalm says all have turned aside and none does good, giving a parallel universal diagnosis.

row.basis: all sin and fall short
row.note: The commentary emphasizes a judgment on humanity as a class; Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory, a comparably universal shortfall.

row.basis: created upright, sought schemes
row.note: The commentary contrasts the human's good created condition with a later loss; Ecclesiastes says God made humanity upright but people sought many schemes.

row.basis: return to dust after mortal labor
row.note: The commentary treats time and the self as capital that finally runs out; the judgment on Adam makes his eating by sweat end in a return to dust.

row.basis: work tested by fire on the day
row.note: The commentary joins work, judgment and a fire storm that can erase a lifetime's produce; Paul says the Day and its fire disclose the quality of each person's work.

row.basis: work lost while person saved
row.note: The commentary's ultimate deficit can be loss of the self; Paul describes a person's work burning and that person suffering loss yet being saved through fire, a narrower outcome for loss.

row.basis: fruit dried by east wind and burned
row.note: The commentary imagines a life's crop ruined by a destructive wind with fire; Ezekiel's vine is uprooted, its fruit dried by the east wind and its branches consumed by fire.

row.basis: storm destroys house without secure foundation
row.note: The commentary opposes a refuge to exposure when destructive weather arrives; Jesus' rain, floods and winds strike the house built on sand, which falls greatly.

row.basis: face reflected in water, heart answered by another
row.note: The commentary's small image of a person seen in another's eye bridges solitary self-knowledge and mutual counsel; the proverb makes a reflected face the analogy for one human heart answering another.

row.basis: reprove neighbor to prevent shared sin
row.note: The commentary's escape from loss includes people recommending truth to one another; Leviticus requires frank correction of a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin because of him.

row.basis: exhort one another every day called Today
row.note: The commentary unites expiring time with reciprocal advice against unnoticed ruin; Hebrews tells believers to exhort one another each day lest sin's deceit harden anyone.

row.basis: mutual stirring toward love and good deeds
row.note: The commentary's exception joins good action to mutual counsel; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to stir love and good works.

row.basis: mortal returned to dust
row.note: The commentary's generic human remains in an ongoing condition of loss; this psalm addresses God as returning mortals to dust, putting humanity inside a bounded mortal state.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary names the generic visible human and asks what loss takes from such a being; the psalm calls the person אֱנוֹשׁ while asking why God remembers him, emphasizing mortal smallness beside divine regard.

row.basis: root table ح ق ق / Hebrew חקק, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary links truth, the appointed day and a life's spent time; Job says a human's days and months are fixed and God has set his limits, using a form of חק for the allotted boundary.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary calls loss an unmeasured deficit in an account; Ecclesiastes says what is lacking, חֶסְרוֹן, cannot be counted, joining deficiency with reckoning while leaving the shortfall unresolved.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's alternative to losing one's capital is right use of it; this proverb says the one who gives to the poor will not lack, using חסר for lack and making generosity the decisive transaction.

row.basis: appointed time to judge every work
row.note: The commentary relates the passing hour to a day that brings each deed to account; Ecclesiastes says God will judge righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work.

row.basis: lack of sense and self-destruction
row.note: The commentary joins failing perception with losing oneself; Proverbs says the adulterer lacks sense and destroys his own life, making a hidden deficit in judgment lead to self-loss.

row.basis: claim to see leaves sin remaining
row.note: The commentary's seeing human may fail to perceive his own loss; Jesus tells his hearers that because they say they see, their sin remains.

row.basis: entrusted money traded to gain more
row.note: The commentary reads the lifetime as trading capital placed in human hands; the first servant immediately trades his master's five talents and gains five more.

row.basis: talent buried in fear
row.note: The commentary distinguishes merely retaining possessions from making a profitable moral return; the fearful servant hides the entrusted talent in the ground and returns only the original sum.

row.basis: unused capital taken away
row.note: The commentary says loss can consume the principal itself; Jesus' conclusion to the talents story says the one who has not will lose even what he has.

row.basis: short day, much work, great wage
row.note: The commentary imagines time as the trader's expiring capital and good deeds as work for gain; R. Tarfon's saying turns the short day, plentiful work and great wage into an urgent moral account.

row.basis: labor incomplete, employer pays wage
row.note: The commentary's exceptions are counted by belief and deeds rather than by ancestry; Avot says one need not finish the work yet may not cease from it, and a faithful employer pays the wage.

row.basis: open shop, ledger, collectors and true judgment
row.note: The commentary's market account and final balance meet Avot's shop on credit, open ledger recording actions, daily collectors and judgment declared true.

row.basis: this world as antechamber, preparation beyond
row.note: The commentary places the human inside a temporal condition whose use determines later gain; Avot calls this world an antechamber and urges preparation there before entering the banquet hall.

row.basis: faith without works is dead
row.note: The commentary notes that the exception from human loss names faith together with good works; James makes the link pointed by declaring faith dead when it has no works.

row.basis: good work and future harvest
row.note: The commentary puts right action against an otherwise diminishing life's work; Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes in due season if one does not give up.

row.basis: wealth flies away when gazed at
row.note: The commentary's rich counter can grow while true capital melts away; Proverbs asks whether one fixes eyes on wealth that vanishes and flies toward heaven.

row.basis: toiler departs with nothing in hand
row.note: The commentary's trader can spend the principal of life and end empty; Ecclesiastes says a person departs naked as he came and takes nothing from his toil in his hand.

row.basis: great wealth destroyed in one hour
row.note: The commentary connects the late hour to a lifetime's accumulated goods lost suddenly; the lament over Babylon says its great wealth has been laid waste in one hour.

row.basis: gain whole world, forfeit life
row.note: The commentary says worldly profit can conceal loss of the person; Mark's version of Jesus' question uses the same economic comparison between gaining the world and forfeiting life.

row.basis: all appear for recompense of deeds
row.note: The commentary's universal human category and final scale lead to deeds being reckoned; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what they have done in the body.

row.basis: death once, then judgment
row.note: The commentary spends the mortal's time toward an appointed day of reckoning; Hebrews places judgment after each human's one death.

row.basis: nothing brought in or taken out
row.note: The commentary contrasts counted goods with the person's last balance; Paul says people brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out.

row.basis: faithful management of small trust
row.note: The commentary uses the orphan's property to connect discerned maturity with entrusted capital; Jesus says reliability in a small matter shows reliability in a great one.

row.basis: trustworthiness with wealth tested
row.note: The commentary's guardian sees whether a ward is ready to receive property; Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to someone unfaithful with unrighteous wealth.

row.basis: minor heir under guardians until set time
row.note: The commentary cites testing an orphan's maturity before releasing property; Paul describes an heir who, while a child, remains under guardians and managers until the father's appointed time.

row.basis: warning not to afflict widow or orphan
row.note: The commentary treats an orphan's property as a trust needing care; Exodus forbids afflicting the vulnerable widow or orphan, supplying the ethical duty behind such guardianship.

row.basis: whole creation pronounced very good
row.note: The commentary contrasts humanity's given good beginning with its later place inside loss; Genesis records God's judgment that all he made was very good.

row.basis: death spread to all people
row.note: The commentary places the human kind, not one individual, under an enveloping negative condition; Paul says death passed to all people after sin entered the world.

row.basis: justification offered after universal shortfall
row.note: The commentary names an exception after its universal verdict; immediately after Paul's statement that all fall short, he says people are justified by grace through Christ, an alternate account of escape.

row.basis: salvation not from works
row.note: The commentary's exception explicitly joins faith with righteous deeds; Paul denies that salvation comes from works, sharpening a difference in how the saving relation of deeds is stated.

row.basis: way of wicked perishes
row.note: The commentary extends loss to losing one's way and finally perishing; the psalm contrasts God's knowledge of the righteous way with the way of the wicked that perishes.

row.basis: broad way leading to destruction
row.note: The commentary's traveler eats through provisions after losing direction and faces ruin; Jesus describes a spacious road on which many travel toward destruction.

row.basis: lost son comes to himself
row.note: The commentary calls the last loss a loss of oneself and also stresses failure to perceive it; the son in the parable comes to himself after dissipating his property and falling into hunger.

row.basis: dead, alive; lost, found
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes loss of property, self and companionship; the father describes the returning son as lost and found and celebrates restored family relation.

row.basis: apparently right road ends in death
row.note: The commentary says the worst loss is the laborer who thinks his route sound; a second proverb states that a seemingly right human way ends in death.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary says the human who can notice things may miss his own deficit; Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful and אנש, desperately sick, then asks who can know it.

row.basis: God searches heart and repays deeds
row.note: The commentary opposes self-deception to an objective account of actions; Jeremiah's next verse says the Lord searches the heart and gives each person according to his ways and deeds.

row.basis: minds blinded against seeing light
row.note: The commentary's named seeing being fails to see the situation he is in; Paul says the minds of unbelievers are blinded so they do not see the gospel's light.

row.basis: clear self-sight before helping brother
row.note: The commentary's reflected self in another's eye leads to reciprocal truth telling; Jesus says first to remove one's own obstruction so one can see clearly to help a brother with his.

row.basis: indirect reflection and eventual face-to-face sight
row.note: The commentary uses a tiny reflected face to describe limited self-knowledge through another person; Paul describes present seeing through a mirror dimly and later face-to-face knowing.

row.basis: friend sharpens friend like iron
row.note: The commentary says the solitary human emerges from loss through others' counsel; Proverbs makes one person sharpen another as iron sharpens iron.

row.basis: acquire a friend and teacher
row.note: The commentary moves from the isolated human to someone who receives truth from another; Avot tells a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, naming relationships as part of moral formation.

row.basis: do not separate from community
row.note: The commentary treats companionship and mutual counsel as an exit from solitary loss; this maxim explicitly warns against separating oneself from the community.

row.basis: encourage and build one another
row.note: The commentary's third verse replaces the isolated figure with mutual exhortation; Paul directs believers to encourage one another and build one another up.

row.basis: bear one another's burdens
row.note: The commentary develops a beast carrying a load and then humans helping each other on the way; Paul converts burden bearing into a reciprocal command among people.

row.basis: root table ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary hears refuge against destruction in the first verse's secondary sense; the plague is עָצַר, stopped, after Phinehas intervenes, offering a concrete image of destruction held back rather than a claim that the Arabic and Hebrew senses are identical.

row.basis: wealth heaped like dust
row.note: The commentary exposes the illusion that ever more counted wealth is safety; Job pictures the wicked heaping silver like dust before describing how another will wear it. Hebrew צבר in the root table is only a sound correspondence to Arabic صبر, not evidence of a shared meaning here.

row.basis: use wealth to make friends and find dwelling
row.note: The commentary makes reciprocal companionship an alternative to loss in the market; Jesus urges using temporary wealth to make friends who will welcome one into lasting dwellings.

row.basis: remember origin, end and final accounting
row.note: The commentary's human has an unseen deficit that an appointed day reveals; Avot asks a person to remember his beginning, his end and before whom he must give account.

row.basis: life and death lead to an account
row.note: The commentary speaks of each human brought to his due day with his deeds; Avot insists that birth, life, death and the eventual account before the divine king are inescapable.

row.basis: hearing and doing make a secure house
row.note: The commentary's refuge against a ruinous storm depends on faith and good action; Jesus compares the one who hears and does his words to a house built on rock.

row.basis: wealth gained quickly dwindles
row.note: The commentary's business account distinguishes growing sums from preserving principal; the proverb says wealth gained hastily diminishes while gathered wealth grows steadily.

row.basis: withheld wages cry against owner
row.note: The commentary's dishonest measure makes another person's principal short; James says wages withheld from harvest laborers cry out, turning economic theft into a charge before God.

row.basis: honest complete weight lengthens days
row.note: The commentary joins accurate scales to one's own final condition; Deuteronomy commands a full and just weight so that the people's days may be long in the land.

row.basis: what one sows, one reaps
row.note: The commentary's lost cultivated produce connects present deeds to a later account; Paul says people reap what they sow, making the harvest an ethical measure.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's generic insan is initially lost but its exception allows another outcome; Daniel sees one like a son of אֱנָשׁ brought before the Ancient of Days, an exalted humanlike figure. The link is limited because Daniel presents a vision figure, not a verdict on humanity as a whole.

row.basis: gathered water and storm clouds
row.note: The commentary imagines loss outside a shelter under destructive weather; David's rescue song pictures God surrounded by gathered water and thick clouds. The root table's Hebrew חשר has a possible sound relation to Arabic خ س ر but the cloud word does not mean loss; this is only an atmospheric image meeting.

row.basis: companionship or death in Honi's return
row.note: The commentary says the human needs others to escape solitary loss; the Honi story ends with his isolation when others do not recognize him and the maxim that one needs companionship or death. This extends the commentary's social image rather than interpreting its verse directly.

row.basis: self-approved ways, God weighs spirits
row.note: The commentary's worst loser thinks his own work good and cannot see his deficit; this proverb says all a person's ways look pure in his own eyes while the Lord weighs the spirits.

row.basis: self-approved way, Lord weighs hearts
row.note: The commentary combines undetected wandering with a final true balance; here every human way seems right to its owner, but the Lord weighs hearts.

row.basis: rich and poor alike light on scales
row.note: The commentary's scale finds the person, not goods, deficient and disregards rank; the psalm calls people of low and high estate alike a breath, rising together on the balance as lighter than breath.

row.basis: just scales belong to the Lord
row.note: The commentary joins the marketplace balance to God's true balance; Proverbs says honest scales and balances are the Lord's, and the weights in a merchant's bag are his work.

row.basis: wicked treasures and short measure
row.note: The commentary's trader accumulates money by reducing another's measure; Micah places ill-gotten treasures beside a scant measure under divine accusation.

row.basis: wicked scales and deceptive weight bag
row.note: The commentary's manipulated weights can appear balanced while cheating the buyer; Micah asks whether one can be acquitted with wicked scales and a bag of deceitful weights.

row.basis: honest weights and measures as covenant duty
row.note: The commentary's two kinds of market fraud involve weighing and measuring; Leviticus commands honest balances, weights, ephah and hin together.

row.basis: large and small measures in one house
row.note: The commentary describes a seller taking full measure but giving short measure; Deuteronomy forbids keeping a large and a small measure at home, extending its adjacent ban on unequal weights to volume.

row.basis: fraud enriches seller by taking the poor
row.note: The commentary says the fraudulent seller reduces another person's capital while growing his own; Amos continues the false-balance scene with merchants buying the poor for silver and selling even grain sweepings.

row.basis: root table خ س ر / Hebrew חסר, sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's loss account can reverse apparent financial gain; Proverbs says one gives freely and increases, while another withholds what is due and comes to מַחְסוֹר, want.

row.basis: appearing rich while possessing nothing
row.note: The commentary separates a cheerful or prosperous appearance from the actual account; Proverbs describes one who pretends to be rich yet has nothing, and another who seems poor yet has great wealth.

row.basis: little with righteousness better than unjust revenues
row.note: The commentary measures profit by righteous action rather than growing receipts; the proverb values a little with righteousness above large revenues gained by injustice.

row.basis: wind passes, bloom and place disappear
row.note: The commentary's storm can erase a lifetime's cultivated produce and the person who owned it; the psalm's wind passes over the mortal's flower so it is gone and its place knows it no more.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary's generic insan spends a mortal lifetime as capital; this psalm calls the human אֱנוֹשׁ and compares his days to grass and his brief flourishing to a field flower.

row.basis: truthful measure sweeps false refuge away
row.note: The commentary connects a true scale with shelter from destructive weather; Isaiah makes justice a measuring line, then says hail will sweep away a refuge of lies and water flood its hiding place.

row.basis: rooted tree bears fruit and prospers in season
row.note: The commentary's alternative to losing a lifetime's crop is good work that survives its allotted time; the righteous person in the psalm is a watered tree yielding fruit in season and prospering in what he does.

row.basis: wicked driven by wind like chaff
row.note: The commentary's lost traveler and ruined crop meet the psalm's contrast: unlike the fruitful rooted tree, the wicked are chaff carried away by the wind.

row.basis: fire at night guides people on their way
row.note: The commentary joins Moses' noticed fire, a night journey and hoped-for guidance; Exodus tells of the Lord leading travelers by a pillar of fire at night so they can travel.

row.basis: human sees surface, God sees heart
row.note: The commentary says a being equipped to see can remain blind to his own real state; Samuel is told humans look at outward appearance while the Lord looks at the heart.

row.basis: fool trusts own way, wise hears advice
row.note: The commentary's mistaken confidence in one's path meets its remedy of counsel from another; the proverb says the fool's way is right in his own eyes but the wise listens to advice.

row.basis: many counselors protect against a fall
row.note: The commentary moves from one human lost alone to people helping one another find a way; the proverb says a people falls without guidance and finds safety in many counselors.

row.basis: two workers gain a better reward
row.note: The commentary joins labor and its wage to companionship as an escape from loss; Ecclesiastes says two are better than one because they have a good reward for their toil.

row.basis: companion lifts the one who falls
row.note: The commentary's lost solitary human needs another's help; Ecclesiastes blesses the one whose companion lifts him after a fall and laments the one alone with no one to lift him.

row.basis: faithful wounds from a friend
row.note: The commentary's true counsel is also likened to an accurate blow that does not miss its mark; the proverb makes even a friend's wounds faithful, giving correction a concrete and costly social form.

row.basis: rich man takes poor man's only lamb
row.note: The commentary's dishonest seller secretly consumes another's principal; Nathan's parable has a rich man spare his own livestock and take the poor man's single cherished lamb instead.

row.basis: another's story exposes one's hidden guilt
row.note: The commentary's seeing human needs another person's truthful address to see himself; after David condemns the parable's rich man, Nathan tells David that he is that man.

row.basis: all deeds including hidden ones judged
row.note: The commentary says loss can grow unseen until a final account reveals it; Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed and every hidden thing, good or evil, into judgment.

row.basis: days of kingdom numbered and ended
row.note: The commentary treats passing time as capital spent toward an appointed reckoning; immediately before Daniel's verdict of deficient weight, he explains that God has numbered the king's days and ended his reign.

row.basis: weighed king loses kingdom
row.note: The commentary says the deficient person can lose far more than goods; immediately after Daniel finds the king lacking on the balance, he declares the kingdom divided and given away.

row.basis: weigh a commandment's loss against reward
row.note: The commentary reads loss and gain as a moral account rather than an emotion; Avot tells a person to reckon the loss of a commandment against its reward and a transgression's reward against its loss.

row.basis: final judgment asks about honest business
row.note: The commentary's market fraud is answered by a later scale for the trader himself; the Talmud says that when one is brought to judgment, one is asked whether one conducted business faithfully.

row.basis: buy true gold and salve for blind eyes
row.note: The commentary joins false wealth to a seeing being who misses his own loss; the speaker follows Laodicea's unrecognized poverty by urging it to buy refined gold and eye salve so it may see.

row.basis: great and small judged from books of deeds
row.note: The commentary's verdict includes every rank and opens a ledger of deeds; Revelation has the dead, great and small, stand before a throne as books are opened and they are judged by recorded works.

row.basis: fool enlarges barns for surplus crops
row.note: The commentary says counted accumulation can mask the loss of life's principal; in the rich fool's own plan, larger barns will hold his abundant grain and goods just before his life is required.

row.basis: stored goods mistaken for years of life
row.note: The commentary's trader mistakes growing assets for safety while time is vanishing; the rich fool tells his soul that goods stored for many years let him rest, eat and drink, an error exposed by the next verse.

row.basis: unseen tomorrow, life as brief vapor
row.note: The commentary's expiring time is capital people cannot safely count in advance; James says they do not know tomorrow and their life appears briefly like vapor before vanishing.

row.basis: earthly treasure eaten and stolen
row.note: The commentary's apparently accumulating store is exposed to real depletion; Jesus warns that earthly treasure is destroyed by moth and rust and broken into by thieves.

row.basis: store lasting treasure elsewhere
row.note: The commentary sets profitable righteous action against perishing capital; Jesus directs hearers to store treasure in heaven, where the losses named in the preceding verse do not consume it.

row.basis: rich in good deeds and generous sharing
row.note: The commentary's exception names good work while money can be lost; Paul tells the wealthy to be rich in good works and ready to share, turning abundance into action for others.

row.basis: good deeds lay up future treasure and life
row.note: The commentary's true balance measures what endures beyond a lifetime; Paul says generous people store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life.

row.basis: give everything yet gain nothing without love
row.note: The commentary links good deeds to reciprocal human relations as the route out of loss; Paul says even giving away all possessions yields no gain if love is absent.

row.basis: enduring good work receives life
row.note: The commentary's rescue from loss joins righteous works with patience; Paul promises eternal life to those who persist in doing good while seeking glory, honor and immortality.

row.basis: endurance after doing God's will
row.note: The commentary's third verse combines good action and mutual counsel in patience; Hebrews says endurance is needed so that, after doing God's will, people receive what was promised.

row.basis: fruit as evidence of repentance
row.note: The commentary sets moral action rather than inherited status as the decisive separation from universal loss; John the Baptist calls for fruit worthy of repentance before confronting reliance on ancestry.

row.basis: Abrahamic descent no guarantee
row.note: The commentary says noble or low origin does not determine who escapes loss; John warns hearers not to presume that having Abraham as father suffices, since God can raise children for him from stones.

row.basis: Abraham's children shown by deeds
row.note: The commentary makes action rather than lineage the visible difference among humans; Jesus answers an appeal to Abrahamic descent by demanding the works of Abraham from those claiming to be his children.

row.basis: man sees his own face in a mirror
row.note: The commentary's reflected little human in another's eye is tied to truthful counsel and action; James compares a hearer who fails to act to a man looking at his own face in a mirror.

row.basis: forgets own face immediately after seeing
row.note: The commentary says a seeing being can miss his own deficit; James' mirror-gazer walks away and at once forgets what he looked like, making self-sight ineffective without lasting response.

row.basis: another turns a wanderer from truth
row.note: The commentary unites truth, a lost path and mutual counsel; James addresses believers whose companion wanders from truth and whom another person turns back.

row.basis: returning wanderer saves life from death
row.note: The commentary says straying can progress from depleted provisions to self-loss; James says one who brings a sinner back from wandering saves a soul from death.

row.basis: gentle correction with self-watchfulness
row.note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel must repair a lost person without forgetting one's own vulnerability; Paul tells the spiritual to restore someone caught in a trespass while watching themselves.

row.basis: younger son receives his estate early
row.note: The commentary cites guardians withholding an orphan's property until maturity is discerned; in Jesus' parable the father gives the younger son his share on request, setting up a different narrative treatment of entrusted capital rather than a competing legal rule.

row.basis: son squanders entrusted property far from home
row.note: The commentary moves from handed-over capital to lost direction and finally self-loss; the younger son leaves home and dissipates his estate in reckless living before he comes to himself.

row.basis: storm cannot ruin house on rock
row.note: The commentary's shelter contrasts with exposure to destructive weather; Jesus' rain, flood and wind strike the house built on rock, but it does not fall because of its foundation.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary's generic insan is a vulnerable being under a sweeping verdict; Job asks what אֱנוֹשׁ is that God magnifies him and attends to him. Job's question concerns oppressive divine attention in its context, making the emotional direction different from the psalmic praise of human regard.

row.basis: every morning and moment tested
row.note: The commentary pictures the person's condition as continuous rather than one past loss; Job complains that God visits and tests him every morning and every moment, a darker continuous scrutiny.

row.basis: root table ء ن س / Hebrew אנש, BDB Arabic cognate
row.note: The commentary's universal human verdict meets Eliphaz's question whether mortal אֱנוֹשׁ can be righteous before God or pure before his maker; the connection is qualified because the claim is made within Eliphaz's disputable speech.

row.basis: high-status human perishes like a beast
row.note: The commentary refuses to separate noble from low human beings in its loss verdict and develops tame and wild animal imagery; the psalm says a human in honor cannot remain and becomes like beasts that perish.

row.basis: rich and poor share one maker
row.note: The commentary's human includes both high and low status before any exception is counted; Proverbs says rich and poor meet together because the Lord is maker of them all.

row.basis: companions resist attack like a strong cord
row.note: The commentary makes connection with others a refuge on the exposed road; Ecclesiastes says two can withstand an attacker and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

row.basis: free choice and judgment by weight of deeds
row.note: The commentary holds a universal condition beside action that distinguishes an exception; R. Akiva's saying in Avot places human choice beside judgment according to the preponderance of deeds.

row.basis: wisdom learned from every person
row.note: The commentary turns the solitary named human toward reciprocal truth telling; Avot calls wise the person who learns from every person, making another human a source of self-correction.

row.basis: true richness as contentment with share
row.note: The commentary warns that counting more possessions can conceal actual loss; the same Avot saying calls rich the person content with his portion, redefining wealth without an expanding hoard.

row.basis: Moses tends flock at Horeb
row.note: The commentary's Qur'anic account sets Moses on a journey with his family when he notices fire; Exodus introduces him tending Jethro's flock at Horeb, a specific change in the scene surrounding the same fire encounter.

row.basis: breath or wind withers the flower
row.note: The commentary's destructive wind erases growth that seemed secure; Isaiah says grass withers and flowers fade when the Lord's breath blows on them, making human flourishing fragile.

row.basis: persevering doer blessed in deed
row.note: The commentary's way out of loss includes action and patience after seeing truth; James contrasts the forgetful mirror-gazer with one who looks into the law, perseveres and acts, receiving blessing in the doing.

row.basis: making use of the time
row.note: The commentary imagines the passing hour as capital available for good work; Ephesians urges readers to make the most of time because the days are evil.

row.basis: desire for riches leads to ruin
row.note: The commentary says financial increase can carry a person toward destruction rather than profit; Paul says those determined to be rich fall into desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.

row.basis: sell possessions for lasting treasure
row.note: The commentary's profitable trade exchanges perishable capital for righteous action; Jesus tells the wealthy man to sell what he has, give to the poor, and gain treasure in heaven.

row.basis: work surviving fire receives reward
row.note: The commentary contrasts the consumed lifetime crop with enduring good work; Paul completes the fire-testing image by saying the builder whose work remains will receive a reward.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The commentary treats loss as a misdirected path that ends in destruction and truth as another way; the Didache opens with two ways, one of life and one of death, rather than treating the error as a mere feeling.

row.basis: unrecognized poverty and self-knowledge
row.note: The commentary says the named seeing human may not perceive his own deficit; Thomas has Jesus say those who fail to know themselves dwell in poverty and are poverty, making an internal condition invisible to its bearer.

row.basis: ways of light and darkness
row.note: The commentary develops losing one's way as a moral loss answered by truthful direction; Barnabas introduces opposing ways of light and darkness. The overlap is the two-path framework, since its particular signs differ from the commentary's trade and scale imagery.
